title: D. AghaBalaSar and Hamed
statement:
You are given a permutation^{∗} p of length n.

For each index i, you may move in one step to:

any index j < i, or

the first index j > i such that p_j > p_i (if such an index exists),

You can always move to any position on the left.

On the right, you can move only to the nearest position whose value is strictly greater than the current one.

Your task is to compute:

∑_{1 ≤ i,j ≤ n} f(i,j).

^{∗}A permutation of length n is an array consisting of n distinct integers from 1 to n in arbitrary order. For example, [2,3,1,5,4] is a permutation, but [1,2,2] is not a permutation (2 appears twice in the array), and [1,3,4] is also not a permutation (n=3 but there is 4 in the array).

Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases t (1 ≤ t ≤ 10^4). The description of the test cases follows.

The first line of each test case contains a single integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^6) — the length of p.

The second line of each test case contains n distinct integers p_1,p_2,…,p_n (1≤ p_i≤ n) — the elements of p.

It is guaranteed that the sum of n over all test cases does not exceed 10^6.

For each test case, print a single integer — the value of ∑limits_{1 ≤ i,j ≤ n} f(i,j).

In the first test case, f(1, 2) + f(2, 1) = 1 + 1 = 2.

In the second test case, f(1, 2) + f(2, 1) = 0 + 1 = 1.

In the third test case, f(1, 2) + f(1, 3) + f(2, 1) + f(2, 3) + f(3, 1) + f(3, 2) = 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 4.

In the fourth test case, f(1, 2) + f(1, 3) + f(2, 1) + f(2, 3) + f(3, 1) + f(3, 2) = 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 7.

Input:
```
6
2
1 2
2
2 1
3
1 3 2
3
1 2 3
5
1 3 5 2 4
7
6 2 4 3 7 5 1
```

Output:
```
2
1
4
7
15
38
```
